summary:
Udmurtia has produced no division-specific transgender evidence in the available sources. A visitor to the republic of Udmurtia stands under the national framework of Russia as it operates countrywide, and the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (version 2.0, June 2025) is the framework against which this division is assessed.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable in Russia and gender-affirming care is banned. The July 2023 law prohibits both gender-affirming surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents, following April and May 2023 proposals to rule out document-only gender changes and to bar reassignment without surgery. ILGA-Europe's 2026 ranking scores Russia at 2%, among the lowest in Europe, with explicit legal limitations making legal gender recognition practically impossible and no self-determination procedure.

The propaganda statutes reach gender transition directly. The 2013 law was expanded in 2022 to apply regardless of age and to prohibit material that makes minors interested in gender transitions.

The Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of the "international LGBT public movement" as extremist applies throughout Russia including Udmurtia, and the movement was added to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organisations on 22 March 2024. Leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols is a criminal offence punishable by prison time, exposing trans visitors to detention, prosecution and imprisonment for visible gender-identity expression, association or advocacy. Enforcement has included arrests of gay club owners, at least one of whom died in custody as of April 2025, and fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag designated as the movement's symbol, including earrings. Between March and May 2026 city courts outlawed nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist, among them Centre T, Coming Out and the Russian LGBT Network.

A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and a single person living abroad may adopt only if that country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition.

Military service rules bear on gender identity. Under the 1 July 2003 military medical expertise statute, people who have problems with their identity and sexual preferences can be drafted only during wartime, with officials stating that non-standard orientation should not be revealed while serving because of the risk of beating; authorities claimed some 2,700 legal gender changes were made recently to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation.

On 30 September 2022 President Vladimir Putin stated it is unacceptable to teach children that instead of men and women there are supposedly some other genders and to offer sex-change surgeries, linking transgender rights abroad to willingness to use all means against Ukraine.

Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people, has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community.

Documented violence includes an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 with 365 fatalities, rising from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015. Premeditated group attacks often using dating apps to hunt homosexuals, led by groups like Occupy Pedophilia, have been active in 40 regions. Chechnya has seen purges since February 2017 with over 100 detained and tortured and at least three extrajudicial killings confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report, leading to EU sanctions on two officials in March 2021.
tangentialFactors:
Consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal after re-legalisation in 1993 with removal of Article 121, and the age of consent is 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation, but same-sex marriages and civil unions are prohibited and a July 2020 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage.

The 2013 law criminalising distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors was expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age.
localsOnly:
Residents of Udmurtia, as in all of Russia, cannot change their legal gender and cannot access gender-affirming care under the 2023 law. The propaganda statutes constrain public expression about gender transition for residents as well as visitors, and the extremist designation applies to residents' association, advocacy and symbol display.

Residents face the same absence of anti-discrimination protection and hate-crime recognition documented nationally, and the military conscription rules on identity and sexual preferences apply to resident draftees.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Udmurtia-specific incidents, enforcement actions, or local institutions concerning transgender people were identified in the available sources; the assessment rests on the national framework as applied to the republic.

The claim that the extremist designation exposes trans visitors to prosecution for visible gender-identity expression is an inference drawn by the source from the designation's scope, not a documented Udmurtia enforcement case.
